source.title: LRM-1B: Towards Large Routing Model
source.authors: Han Li; Fei Liu; Zhen-Kun Wang; Qing-Fu Zhang

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figure and table formatting is flattened, but the scaling results are also described in the text and detailed tables.
record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling analysis to reinforcement-learning vehicle-routing solvers and reports performance-gap scaling with model size and inference resources; it does not test language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling work as motivation, but its own experiments concern routing-model performance gaps, not language-model cross-entropy. It does not test token scaling or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Rows record the routing-model scaling results and the reported out-of-training-range performance issue.
record.test_reason: It trains RL routing transformers from 1.3M to 1.1B parameters and fits a power law of solution gap against parameter count. That is a scaling-law test in a new training regime, so it bears on V5 only. It has no language-model loss, token scaling or compute-optimal split. The inference-compute scaling it reports is a related but different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors report power laws of routing gap against model size (1M–1B), inference trajectories and inference compute. They state that LRM-1B is SOTA on synthetic benchmarks. On real-world CVRPLib the 40M model is best and the 1B model is worse, which they attribute to overfitting the demand–capacity ratio.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains RL vehicle-routing solvers and measures solution gaps and inference resources, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy, training tokens, or training compute. Its model-size fit uses OLS on routing performance gaps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported fit strength varies with test difficulty; the authors note diminishing returns from 40M to 1B in Uniform50 but a closer power-law trend in harder OOD settings. Inference results also vary with trajectory count and use of ×8 augmentation. Real-world performance depends on the demand-capacity ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: Solution gap falls as a power law in inference trajectories (aT≈0.058–0.101) and inference GFLOPs (aC≈0.095–0.114, mean 0.106). Returns diminish above ~10^3 GFLOPs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-time compute (sampling/augmentation) scaling follows a power law in neural combinatorial solvers.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger models reach lower Uniform100 gap with the same number of gradient steps (Fig. 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models are more sample-efficient during training.

record.problems: The scaling study uses four model sizes and performance gap rather than language-model cross-entropy. Model size changes alongside architectural configuration, and the study does not compare training-token or training-compute allocations. Some fitted values are available only in figures. The 1B model underperforms the 40M model on the reported real-world generalization issue.
record.rows_left_out: The raw inference trajectory and compute grids in Appendix D, Tables 8–10, are not itemized; the fitted exponents and key per-model-size results are recorded instead. The training data-efficiency curves (Figure 9) and general solver comparisons are omitted because they do not report a power-law result for a version beyond the scaling outcomes captured here.

untested.parts: Data and training-compute scaling (the authors list this as future work), other modalities (image/video), repeated data, fine-tuning/transfer, and loss rather than a solution-gap metric.
All of it; there is no language-model pretraining loss.
All of it; no extrapolation from small fits is tested.
All of it; there is no parameter/token allocation.
All of it; shape varies together with size.

missing.what: Per-model-size real-world gaps across CVRPLib suites (1M/5M/40M/1B, plus baselines). Examples: X 700–1000, 40M 14.909% vs 1B 37.527%; F, 40M 5.485% vs 1B 10.289%.
Per-test-set fitted αN and R² for model-size scaling (e.g. Uniform50 0.071/R² 0.899, Uniform100 0.057/0.907, OOD50 0.073/0.921). Only the average is recorded.

record.verdict_notes: The measure is gap to HGS, a task metric, not loss. Only four sizes are tested, and architecture and optimizer change with size. The paper attributes αN=0.076 to Hoffmann et al., but it comes from Kaplan. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy versus parameters, tokens, or training compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from smaller-run loss fits.
The loss-minimising parameter/token split at fixed training compute.
Isolated comparisons of architectures at fixed parameter count.
Language-model cross-entropy, image/video modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer. The tested setting is RL-trained routing models and solver performance gaps.
Downstream language-model task performance and its relationship to pretraining loss.
Whether language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on parameter counting, training schedule, data, or fitting choices.

rows.subject: LRM-1B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated performance gaps on real-world CVRPLib instances across demand-capacity ratios.
rows.baseline: LRM-40M; exact paired values not stated in the accompanying text
rows.value: Gap increases sharply as R grows; the authors attribute this to overfitting to the training-time R range.
rows.locator: Appendix D, Figure 8 and accompanying text
rows.note: The paper states that the 40M model generalizes across the plotted R values, while the 1B model's gap rises on unseen ratios.
rows.check: Recorded as partial, but the 1B model is worse than the 40M model on real-world data (Table 11, Fig. 8). Larger scale reverses the gain here. The baseline is the 40M model, not HGS.
